issues.legal_issue: The High Court’s power to take suo motu cognizance of criminal contempt of a subordinate court is not excluded when the statutory modes of reference or motion are not used.
material_facts: The alleged contempt arose in proceedings before a Member of the Board of Revenue, which the Court held was a court subordinate to the High Court.
The High Court was moved by a petition from an advocate, rather than by a reference from the subordinate court or a motion by the Advocate-General or notified Law Officer.
issues.conclusion: Section 15(2) does not restrict the High Court’s power to take cognizance of and punish criminal contempt of a subordinate court on its own motion.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 129 and 215 preserve the Supreme Court’s and High Court’s powers as Courts of Record; Parliament may define and limit those powers and regulate procedure under Entries 77 of List I and 14 of List III of the Seventh Schedule. Section 10 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 gives the High Court the same jurisdiction, power, authority, procedure and practice for contempt of subordinate courts as for contempt of itself. Reading Section 15(2) harmoniously with Section 10, and consistently with the reasoning in Mohd. Ikram Hussain v. The State of U.P., Section 15(2) does not remove the High Court’s suo motu power.

predicates.subordinate_court_criminal_contempt: The alleged conduct is criminal contempt connected with a court subordinate to the High Court.
predicates.statutory_reference_or_authorized_motion: The High Court has not been moved by a reference from the subordinate court or by an authorized motion.

issues.definition: When alleged criminal contempt concerns a subordinate court and no reference or authorized motion has been made, the High Court still retains power to take cognizance on its own motion.

issues.legal_issue: A private petition may provide information on which the High Court exercises its discretion to take suo motu cognizance of subordinate-court contempt, subject to safeguards against frivolous or insignificant proceedings.
material_facts: An advocate who had appeared before the Board of Revenue filed a petition directly in the High Court and asked it to act suo motu.
The petition alleged that the Member of the Board had abused the advocate during the hearing and ordered a court peon to remove him; the Member denied the allegations.

The High Court issued notice, and the Supreme Court concluded that, in the circumstances, the High Court had not acted improperly or illegally by taking suo motu cognizance on the advocate’s petition.
issues.conclusion: The High Court may, in its discretion, act suo motu on information in a private petition, and it did not act improperly or illegally in doing so in this case. The Supreme Court expressed no view on the merits of the contempt allegation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 does not prescribe the sources of information on which the High Court may act suo motu. A private petition may be refused or treated as information for suo motu action; the High Court may act especially where the petitioner is a responsible member of the legal profession and requests such action. Cognizance should be taken only where the information is prima facie not frivolous and the alleged contempt is not merely technical or trivial, and this course should be used sparingly for grave and serious contempt. The procedural modes protect court time from frivolous complaints; the Court also referred to the Sanyal Committee’s view that action on a motion by another agency can provide assurance to the person charged and the public.

rule.if: subordinate_court_criminal_contempt and private_petition_supplies_information and responsible_legal_petitioner and petition_requests_suo_motu and information_prima_facie_nonfrivolous and allegation_not_technical_or_trivial and alleged_contempt_grave_or_serious

predicates.subordinate_court_criminal_contempt: The alleged conduct is criminal contempt connected with a court subordinate to the High Court.
predicates.private_petition_supplies_information: A private person’s petition provides the High Court with information about the alleged contempt.
predicates.responsible_legal_petitioner: The petitioner is a responsible member of the legal profession.
predicates.petition_requests_suo_motu: The petitioner asks the High Court to act on its own motion.
predicates.information_prima_facie_nonfrivolous: The High Court is prima facie satisfied that the information is not frivolous.
predicates.allegation_not_technical_or_trivial: The alleged contempt is not merely technical or trivial.
predicates.alleged_contempt_grave_or_serious: The alleged contempt is of a grave and serious nature.

issues.definition: When information about alleged subordinate-court criminal contempt is supplied in a petition by a responsible legal professional who requests suo motu action, and the allegation is prima facie nonfrivolous, nontrivial, grave and serious, the High Court may choose to take cognizance on its own motion.
